web_evidence.title: An Allegorical Reading: Arundhati Roy’s The God of Small Things
web_evidence.note: The university-hosted master’s-thesis abstract describes an omniscient narrator who supplies events unavailable to Rahel while filtering the two timelines through character memory.

web_evidence.title: Reading the Language of Children in Arundhati Roy’s The God of Small Things
web_evidence.note: This scholarly article distinguishes the twins’ childlike perspective from an omniscient narrator and explains that the perspectives alternate within the narration rather than becoming first-person base sections.

web_evidence.title: Re-Membering Personal History in The God of Small Things
web_evidence.note: The scholarly essay explicitly associates the novel’s time shifts with third-person narration and analyzes shifting focalization among the twins and adults within that narration.

web_evidence.title: The God of Small Things
web_evidence.note: The reference essay explicitly identifies an omniscient third-person narrator grounded in Rahel’s memories and traces that narrator across the novel’s chapters.

web_evidence.title: From sweaty to sultry: why fiction loves a heatwave
web_evidence.note: Penguin reproduces the novel’s environmental opening, but that passage is person-unmarked and therefore only verifies the opening text, not the book-level person.

Searched Google Books, Penguin Random House, Penguin UK, university repositories, scholarly PDFs, journal sites, and reference sources for sustained or whole-book evidence.

Opened Penguin Random House and Google Books preview pages; the PRH sample control was not exposed and Google Books returned mainly bibliographic or limited-preview material, so neither was used as diagnostic person evidence.

Opened the Taylor & Francis DOI for "The Small Voice of History" after its search extract explicitly described third-person handling of multiple perspectives, but the page returned HTTP 403, so it was omitted from web_evidence.
No opened credible source described sustained first- or second-person base sections; sources consistently treated changes of perspective as third-person focalization.
person_note: The Goodreads evidence repeatedly shows a nonparticipating narrator referring to Rahel, Estha, Ammu, Velutha, and others externally while entering several characters’ thoughts. Multiple scholarly whole-book analyses independently identify the narration as omniscient or close third person and explain that its shifting child/adult perspectives are focalization within third-person narration, not changes to first-person base narration. The conspicuous “I,” “we,” and “you” forms occur in an authorial nonfiction quotation, gnomic statements, or character speech and therefore do not create alternate base sections. Some short or clipped quotations remain locally unmarked or unclear, but they do not conflict with the sustained third-person passages. The main nuance is the narrator’s unusually close alignment with Rahel’s and Estha’s language and memories; the researched structural evidence resolves that nuance as third person.
